To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the weight of human lungs is not a suitable diagnostic criterium for the distinction of normal lungs from lungs of shock victims.

lung weight is a useful diagnostic criterium, that the normal lung weight is about one half of the value given in the literature, and that the weight of lungs is influenced by the survival time of the patient.

the lung weight of patients dying from extrathoracic multiple trauma may be significantly elevated, and that the determination of the "true" normal lung weight is a problem that requires further investigation.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the problems of the determination of the "norm" of the lung weight and with the influence of the duration of shock on the lung weight, the extravascular lung water content, the hemoglobin content, and the DNA content.
the question of how the "normal" weight of the lung can be determined, and with a comparison of the weight of normal lungs with that of shock lungs.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the lung weight of a patient dying from extrathoracic multiple trauma is elevated in relation to the weight of a normal lung if the lung is not congested or edematized.
the weight of the human lungs is an important diagnostic criterion for the evaluation of the state of the lungs.
the "normal" weight of human lungs is about 234 g (average) and is not 400-500 g as is generally accepted.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the weight of the lung, which is an easy and quick method for the pathologist, can be used as a diagnostic criterian for the distinction of shock lungs from normal lungs.
the weight of human lungs can be used as a diagnostic criterion only in combination with histologic, biochemical and morphometric investigations.
the weight of human lungs is not a suitable diagnostic criterium.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the weight of lungs should not be used as a diagnostic criteria for the presence of interstitial edema or for the diagnosis of pulmonary contusions.
the weight of human lungs is a very useful diagnostic criterium.
